This matter comes before the Public Service Commission of South Carolina
(Commission) upon the Application of Velocity IG Operations, LLC (Velocity IG or
Company) for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) to provide
facilities-based and resold local exchange and interexchange (including exchange access)
telecommunications services within the State of South Carolina (Application). Velocity IG
also seeks alternative and flexible regulation, and a waiver of the application of certain
Commission regulations,
as described below.
For the
reasons
set forth below, the
Commission approves the Application and grants the relief requested therein.
I.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Velocity IG filed the Application on March 6, 2026, pursuant to S.C. Code Ann.
section 58-9-280 and the applicable rules and regulations of the Commission. In the
Application, the Company requested that the Commission issue
a
CPCN and regulate the
Company’s interexchange
service offerings
in
accordance with
the principles
and 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
- ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE2
procedures established for alternative regulation in Commission Order Nos. 95-1734 and
96-55 in Docket No. 95-661-C, and as modified by Commission Order No. 2001-997 in
Docket No. 2000-407-C. The Company also requested flexible regulation of its local
exchange service offerings pursuant to Order No. 98-165 in Docket No. 97-467-C. Finally,
the Company requested: a waiver of the requirement in S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-610 that
all records required under the rules be kept within the State; that the Company be exempt
from any recordkeeping rules or regulations that might require a carrier to maintain its
financial records in conformance with the Uniform System of Accounts (USOA),
as
required in S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-611; and a waiver of the requirement in S.C. Code
Ann. Regs. 103-631 that the Company be responsible for having its customers listed in a
telephone directory.!
On March 20, 2026, the Commission Clerk’s Office issued a letter instructing
Applicant to publish,
one time,
a Notice of Filing and Public Hearing (Notice) in
newspapers of general circulation in the areas of the state affected by the Application. The
Notice contained information regarding the Application, the date and location of the
hearing on the Application, and the manner in which stakeholders could participate in the
case. The Company published the Notice as required and, on April 6, 2026, filed Affidavits
of Publication.
On March 9, 2026, Donna L. Rhaney, Esquire, and Jasmine C. Gunning, Esquire,
entered a Notice of Appearance on behalf of the South Carolina Office of Regulatory Staff
' The Application also contains
a request for confidential treatment of certain commercially sensitive
financial information attached as Confidential Exhibit C to its Application. This request was granted by Order
No. 2026-74-H, issued on March 18, 2026. 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
- ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 3
(ORS).? On March 20, 2026, the Palmetto Broadband Coalition (PBC) filed a Petition to
Intervene, which was granted on April 3, 2026, by Order No. 2026-84-H. The Company
and PBC reached a Stipulation, which was filed on March 24, 2026, and is attached hereto
as Order Exhibit No. 1.
On April 3, 2026, the Company filed the Direct Testimony of Bill Cook, Chairman
of Operations for Velocity IG. On April 28, 2026, counsel for ORS filed a letter (ORS
Letter) with the Commission stating that ORS did not object to the approval of the
Application and did not intend to present any witnesses or attend the hearing scheduled in
this proceeding. Letter from Jasmine C. Gunning, Esquire, ORS, to the Honorable Jocelyn
G. Boyd, Chief Clerk & Executive Director, Commission (April 28, 2026). On May 28,
2026, the Company submitted selected Confidential Financial Statements of Columbia
Capital Equity Partners VII-A, L.P., along with a request for confidential treatment of the
same.?
A hearing was held on June 1, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. before
a Commission-appointed
Hearing Examiner.* The Company was represented by John J. Pringle, Jr., Esquire. PBC
and ORS did not appear at the hearing. At the start of the hearing, the Application and
Exhibits thereto, the Stipulation, and the ORS Letter were entered into evidence. The
prefiled Direct Testimony of Bill Cook was entered into the record as if given orally from
? Pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. section 58-4-10(B), the Office of Regulatory Staff is a party of record in all
filings, applications, and proceedings before the Commission.
3 The request for confidential treatment was granted by Order No. 2026-125-H, issued on June 1, 2026.
‘The hearing was continued to this date pursuant to Order No. 2026-117-H, issued on May 14, 2026, granting
the Company’s request for a continuance.

the stand. Finally, Mr. Cook, appearing via video conference, sponsored his prefiled Direct
Testimony and answered questions from counsel and the Hearing Examiner.
II.
FINDINGS OF FACT
After considering the Application (including the exhibits submitted therewith),
Stipulation, ORS Letter, and all other applicable filings in the Docket, as well as the
testimony and other evidence presented
at the hearing, the Commission makes the
following findings of fact:
1.
The Company is a limited liability company organized under the laws ofthe
State of Delaware and authorized to do business in the State of South Carolina.
2.
The Company seeks authority to provide facilities-based and resold local
exchange and interexchange (including exchange access) telecommunications services in
South Carolina.
3.
The Company has the managerial, technical, and financial resources to
provide the services requested.
4.
The services to be provided meet the service standards of the Commission.
5.
The Company’s provision of services
will
not adversely impact the
availability of affordable local exchange service.
6.
The Company will support universally available telephone service
at
affordable rates.
7.
The Company’s provision of services will not adversely impact the public
interest.
8.
The Stipulation between the PBC and the
Company is in the public interest. 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
—- ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 5
9.
Following the execution of the Stipulation, PBC does not oppose granting
a Certificate to the Company.
10.
ORS does not object to the relief requested in the Application.
11. | The Company requests a waiver ofthe requirement in S.C. Code Ann. Regs.
103-610
that all records be kept within the State. The Company maintains its records at its
principal offices in Virginia and states that maintaining a separate set ofbooks and records
in South Carolina would be unduly costly and burdensome. The Commission finds the
Company’s requested waiver reasonable and understands the potential difficulty presented
to the Company should the waiver not be granted. Further, the Commission finds that a
waiver of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-610 1s not contrary to the public interest.
12.
Regarding S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-611, the Company requests that it be
exempt from any recordkeeping rules or regulations that might require a carrier to maintain
its financial records in conformance with the USOA. Applicant maintains its books in
accordance
with
Generally
Accepted
Accounting
Principles
(GAAP),
which
the
Commission finds appropriate for the manner in which Applicant is regulated. Further, the
Commission finds that a waiver of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-611 is not contrary to the
public interest.
13.
The Company seeks a waiver of the requirement of S.C. Code Ann. Regs.
103-631 that a utility have its customers listed in a telephone directory. The Company does
not intend to provide retail residential local exchange services and states that to the extent
that the Company provides such services in the future, the Company will contract with at
least one incumbent local exchange carrier (or its directory publishing affiliate) for the 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 6
inclusion of the Company’s
customer databases
in
an appropriate directory.
The
Commission finds that the requested waiver of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-631 is reasonable
and not contrary to the public interest.
14. | The Company does not currently intend to offer voice service and will not
provide
retail residential
local exchange service. Therefore,
the requirement
for
a
performance bond or other security measure, as set forth in S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-607,
does not apply to the Company. Should the Company offer residential local exchange
services in the future in South Carolina, the Commission finds that the Company will be
required to comply with S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-607.
IJ.
EVIDENCE IN SUPPORT OF FINDINGS OF FACT
The record reveals that the Company is a limited liability company organized under
the laws of the State of Delaware and authorized to do business in the State of South
Carolina. Application at 3, Exhibit A.
According to Mr. Cook, the Company seeks authority as a provider of facilities-
based
and
resold local
exchange
and
interexchange
(including exchange
access)
telecommunications services. Cook Direct at 3:15-17. Mr. Cook explained the Company’s
request for authority, and the record further reveals the Company’s services, operations,
and marketing procedures.
The Company will provide point-to-point telecommunications services such as
Private Line and similar services to wholesale customers (e.g., other carriers and providers)
and enterprise customers. /d. at 5:8-12. The Company plans to construct an underground,
high fiber count network to provide dark fiber and communications services to and from 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE7
carrier-neutral facilities and points-of-presence. /d. at 5:12-14. The Company will provide
fiber optic connectivity between various locations throughout South Carolina, and its
services will support a variety of customers, including enterprise, wireless and wireline
carriers, government entities, and data centers. /d. at 5:15-17. The Company may utilize
leases and indefeasible rights of use agreements with other carriers and thus seeks authority
to provide service via resale arrangements. /d. at 6:9-11. Velocity IG does not currently
plan to offer voice service and will not provide retail residential local exchange service. Jd.
at 10:14; see id. at 7:19-8:3.
Mr. Cook also discussed the Company’s technical, financial, and managerial
resources to provide the services for which it seeks authority. Mr. Cook offered that the
Company possesses sufficient financial
resources to support its operations in South
Carolina. /d. at 4:21-22. The Company also submitted its most recent balance sheet and
income statement
as Confidential Exhibit C to the Application. /d.
at 4:22-5-1. The
Company also provided confidential financial statements of the Company’s tndirect parent
company for the year ending December 31, 2025. /d. at 5:1-5.
Concerning its management and technical capabilities, the Company’s Application
and Mr. Cook’s testimony both evidence that the Company’s management has extensive
experience in telecommunications,
information technology, regulatory matters,
and
accounting and finance. Application, Exhibit D; Cook Direct at 4:5-19. Biographies of the
Company’s management team, as filed with the Application, demonstrate that they have
significant experience working in the industry. Application, Exhibit D. Mr. Cook also 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 8
testified
that
the Company
would operate
in
accordance with
Commission rules,
regulations, guidelines, and Commission Orders. Cook Direct at 8:4-9.
Mr. Cook offered that approval of the Company’s Application would serve the
public interest. /d. at 11:19-12:8. He indicated that granting the Application would increase
competition, which would, inter alia, drive prices closer to costs and promote efficiency in
the delivery of services and in the development of new services. /d.
The Company requested
a waiver of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-610,
as the
Company’s books are maintained at its operational headquarters in Alexandria, Virginia.
Application at 7. Further, the Company requested an exemption from record keeping
policies that require maintenance of financial records in conformance with the Uniform
System of USOA. /d. at 7-8. The Company maintains its books in accordance with GAAP.
Id. at 8. Additionally, the Company seeks a waiver of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-631 so
that it will not be required to publish local exchange directories. Jd. To the extent that the
Company provides retail local exchange service in the future, the Company will contract
with at least one incumbent local exchange carrier (or its directory publishing affiliate) for
the inclusion ofthe Company’s customer databases in an appropriate directory. /d. Further,
the Company does not intend to provide retail residential local exchange services in South
Carolina at this time, but should it do so in the future, the Company will meet the bond
requirements (or seek
an appropriate waiver)
of S.C.
Code
Ann.
Regs.
103-607.
Application at 4.

IV.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Having considered the applicable statues, regulations, and Commission orders, and
based upon the Findings of Fact set forth above, the Commission makes the following
Conclusions of Law:
l.
As required by S.C. Code Ann. section 58-9-280(B)(1), the Company
possesses the managerial, technical, and financial resources sufficient to provide the
telecommunications services as described in its Application.
2.
Pursuant to the requirement of S.C. Code Ann. section 58-9-280(B)(2), the
Company will provide services which will meet the service standards of the Commission.
3.
In accordance with S.C. Code Ann. section 58-9-280(B)(3), provision ofthe
service
as described in the Application will not adversely impact the availability of
affordable local exchange service.
4.
As required by S.C. Code Ann. section 58-9-280(B)(4), the Company will
participate in the support of universally available telephone service at affordable rates to
the extent that the Company may be required to do so by the Commission.
5.
Pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. section 58-9-280(B)(5), provision ofthe service
as described in the Application will not adversely impact the public interest.
6.
The Company’s Application to provide resold and facilities-based local
exchange and interexchange telecommunications services within South Carolina will serve
the public interest by providing for efficient use of existing telecommunications resources.
7.
Issuance of the authority to provide local exchange and interexchange
telecommunications services
as requested by the Company and
as
set forth in its 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 10
Application and Mr. Cook’s testimony is in the best interests of the citizens of the State of
South Carolina.
8.
A CPCN should be granted to the Company to provide facilities-based and
resold intrastate local exchange and interexchange telecommunications services.
9.
The Company’s local exchange telecommunications services shall be
regulated in accordance with the principles and procedures established for flexible
regulation first granted to NewSouth Communications by Order No. 98-165 in Docket No.
97-467-C. Specifically, the Commission adopts for the Company’s competitive intrastate
local exchange services
a rate structure incorporating maximum rate levels with the
flexibility for adjustment below the maximum rate levels approved by the Commission.
Further, the Company’s local exchange service tariff filings are presumed valid upon filing.
An investigation of the tariff filing may be instituted within thirty days of the tariff filing,
in which
case the tariff filing would be suspended pending further Order of the
Commission. If an investigation is instituted on a particular tariff filing, notice of the
investigation will be provided to the person or entity making the tariff filing and to the
Commission. The notice is timely if dated within thirty days of the filing date. Further, any
such tariff filings will be subject to the same monitoring process as similarly situated local
exchange carriers.
10.
Should the Company offer residential interexchange services in the future,
the Commission adopts a rate design for the Company for its residential interexchange
services which include maximum rate levels for each tariff charge. A rate structure
incorporating maximum rate levels with the flexibility for adjustment below the maximum 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
~ ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 11
rate levels has been previously adopted by the Commission. /n Re: Application of GTE
Sprint Communications Corporation, etc., Order No. 84-622, issued in Docket No. 84-10-
C (Aug. 2, 1984).
11.
Should the Company offer residential interexchange services in the future,
the Company shall not adjust its residential interexchange rates for end-users below the
approved maximum level without notice to the Commission and to the public. The
Company shall file its proposed rate changes, publish its notice of such changes, and file
affidavits of publication with the Commission two weeks prior to the effective date of the
changes. However, the public notice requirement is waived, and therefore not required, for
reductions below the maximum cap in instances which do not affect the general body of
subscribers or do not constitute a general rate reduction. Jn Re: Application of GTE Sprint
Communications, etc., Order No. 93-638, issued in Docket No. 84-10-C (July 16, 1993).
Any proposed increase in the maximum rate level for residential interexchange services
reflected in the tariff which would be applicable to the general body of the Company's
subscribers shall constitute
a general ratemaking proceeding and will be treated in
accordance with the notice and hearing provisions of S.C. Code Ann. section 58-9-540.
12.
The Commission concludes that any intrastate interexchange business
telecommunications services offered by the Company shall be regulated in accordance with
the principles and procedures established for alternative regulation of business service
offerings
set
out in Order Nos.
95-1734 and 96-55 in Docket No.
95-661-C. The
Commission has previously granted this “alternative regulation” to competitive intrastate
interexchange carriers operating within South Carolina, and the Commission concludes 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 12
that the competitive marketplace requires the Commission to allow this flexible regulation
to those carriers which request it. Specifically, the Commission-approved alternative
regulation allows business service offerings, including
consumer card services and
operator services, to be subject to a relaxed regulatory scheme identical to that granted to
AT&T Communications in Order Nos. 95-1734 and 96-55 in Docket No. 95-661-C.
However, pursuant to Order No. 2001-997 (Docket No. 2000-407-C), this Commission has
modified alternative regulation by the re-imposition of rate caps with regard to certain
“operator-assisted calls” where a customer uses a local exchange carrier’s calling card to
complete calls from locations which have not selected that local exchange carrier as the
toll provider. Order No. 2001-997, dated November 8, 2001, imposed a maximum cap of
$1.75 for operator surcharges for such calls, and a maximum cap of $0.35 related to the
flat per-minute rate associated with these calls. Under this relaxed regulatory scheme, tariff
filings for business services shall be presumed valid upon filing. The Commission will
have seven days in which to institute an investigation ofany tariff filing. Ifthe Commission
institutes an investigation of a particular tariff filing within the seven days, the tariff filing
will then be suspended until further order of the Commission.
13.
Pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-601(3), the Company’s request for
waiver of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-610 should be granted, as strict compliance with the
regulation potentially causes undue hardship on the Company and granting the waiver is
not contrary to the public interest.
14.
The Company’s request, pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-601(3), for
waiver of any record-keeping rules or regulations contemplated by S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 13
103-611 that might require the Company to keep its records in conformance with the
USOA should also be granted, as strict compliance would potentially cause undue hardship
on the Company and granting the waiver is not contrary to the public interest.
15.
In accordance with S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-601(3), the Company’s
request for waiver of the requirements of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-631 that a utility have
its customers listed in a telephone directory should be granted, as the Company does not
intend to provide retail residential local exchange services. To the extent that the Company
provides such services in the future, the Company should be required to contract with at
least one incumbent local exchange carrier (or its directory publishing affiliate) for the
inclusion of the Company’s customer databases in an appropriate directory. The requested
waiver of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-631 is not contrary to the public interest.
16.
The Stipulation between the Company and PBC attached as Order Exhibit
No. | should be approved, with its terms incorporated herein.
V.
ORDERING PROVISIONS
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED THAT:
1.
The Stipulation between the Company and PBC attached as Order Exhibit
No.
1 is hereby approved, with its terms incorporated herein.
2.
The Application is approved and a Certificate of Public Convenience and
Necessity
to provide facilities-based
and
resold
local exchange
and interexchange
telecommunications services within the State of South Carolina is hereby granted to the
Company. 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 14
3.
The regulatory treatment adopted for the Company’s services shall conform
to the design described in Conclusions of Law above.
4.
If it has not already done so, the Company shall file its revised tariffutilizing
the Commission’s e-filing system for tariffs within thirty days ofthe issuance ofthis Order.
The revised tariff should be electronically filed in a text searchable PDF format using the
Commission’s DMS System (http://dms.psc.sc.gov). An additional copy should be sent via
email
to etariff@psc.sc.gov
to
be
included
in
the
Commission’s
ETariff System
(http://etariff.psc.sc.gov). Future revisions to the tariff should be made using the ETariff
System. The revised tariff shall be consistent with the findings of this Order and shall be
consistent with the Commission’s Rules and Regulations.
5.
The Company shall resell the services regulated by this Commission ofonly
those local exchange carriers (LECs) authorized to do business in South Carolina by this
Commission.
6.
The Company shall file annual financial information in the form of annual
reports and gross receipts reports as required by the Commission. The annual report and
the gross receipt report will necessitate the filing of intrastate information. Therefore, the
Company shall keep financial records on an intrastate basis for South Carolina to comply
with the annual report and gross receipts filings. The proper form for filing annual financial
information can be found at ORS’s website at http://ors.sc.gov. The title of this form is
“Telecommunications Company Annual Report.” This form shall be utilized by the
Company to file annual financial information with the Commission and ORS and shall be
filed no later than April 1 of each year. 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 15
7.
Commission gross receipts forms are due to be filed with the Commission
and ORS no later than August 31 of each year. The proper form for filing gross receipts
information can be found at the ORS website at http://ors.sc.gov, and the appropriate form
is entitled “Gross Receipts Form.”
8.
Each telecommunications company certified in South Carolina is required
to file annually with ORS the Universal Service Fund (USF) worksheet, which may be
found on the ORS website at http://ors.sc.gov. This worksheet provides ORS information
required to determine each telecommunications company’s liability to the State USF fund.
The USF worksheet is due to be filed annually no later than August 1 with ORS.
9.
The Company shall, in compliance with Commission regulations, designate
and maintain an authorized utility representative who is prepared to discuss, on a regulatory
level, customer relations (complaint) matters, engineering operations, tests, and repairs. In
addition, the Company shall provide the Commission and ORS in writing the name of the
authorized representative to be contacted in connection with general management duties as
well as emergencies which occur during non-office hours. The Company shall file the
names, addresses, and telephone numbers of these representatives with the Commission
and ORS within thirty days ofreceipt ofthis Order. The “Authorized Utility Representative
Information” form can be found at the Commission’s website at https://psc.sc.gov/forms.
This form shall be utilized for the provision of this information to the Commission and
ORS. Further, the Company shall promptly notify the Commission and ORS in writing if
the representatives are replaced. 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
— ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 16
10.
The Company is directed to comply with all Rules and Regulations of the
Commission, unless a regulation is specifically waived by the Commission.
11.
The requested waiver of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-610 is hereby granted.
However, the Company shall make available its books and records at all reasonable times
upon request by ORS, and the Company shall promptly notify the Commission and ORS
if the location of its books and records change.
12.
The
requested
waiver
of
any
record-keeping
rules
or
regulations
contemplated by S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-611 that might require the Company to keep
its records in conformance with the USOA is granted. The Company shall maintain its
financial records in conformance with GAAP.
13. | The requested waiver of the requirements of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-631
that a utility have its customers listed in a telephone directory is granted. To the extent that
the Company provides retail residential services in the future, the Company shall contract
with at least one incumbent local exchange carrier (or its directory publishing affiliate) for
the inclusion of the Company’s customer databases in
an appropriate directory,
or
otherwise comply with the provisions of S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-631.
14.
The Company need not file a bond pursuant to S.C. Code Regs. 103-607
until such time as the Company provides retail residential local exchange service in South
Carolina.
15.
In the event that the Company offers or provides any service that would
implicate Title 23, Chapter 47 of the South Carolina Code Annotated, the Company is
required to comply with that Title and Chapter, which governs the establishment and 

DOCKET NO. 2026-66-C
—- ORDER NO. 2026-364
JULY 1, 2026
PAGE 17
implementation of a “Public Safety Communications Center,” which is more commonly
known as a “911” system or “911 service.” Services available through a 911 system include
law enforcement, fire, and emergency medical services. In recognition of the necessity of
quality 911 services being provided to the citizens of South Carolina, in the event the
Company offers or provides the appropriate services, the Commission hereby instructs the
Company to contact the appropriate authorities regarding 911 service in the counties and
cities where the Company will be operating, should the Company become interconnected
to the public switched telephone network. Contact with the appropriate 911
service
authorities is to be made before voice or dial tone service in South Carolina. By this Order
and prior to providing voice or dial tone services within South Carolina, the Company shall
contact the 911 coordinator in each county, as well as the 911 Coordinator in each city
where the city has its
own 911 system and shall provide information regarding the
Company’s operations as required by the 911 system.
16.
This Order shall remain in full force and effect until further Order of the
Commission.

The Palmetto Broadband Coalition (“PBC”) (see attachment “A” for list of companies) and
Velocity IG Operations, LLC (“Velocity IG Operations” or “Applicant”) hereby enter into the
following stipulations. As a consequence of these stipulations and conditions, PBC does not oppose
Velocity IG Operations Application. PBC and Applicant stipulate and agree as follows:
!,
PBC does not oppose the granting of a Certificate of Public Convenience and
Necessity to Applicant, provided the South Carolina Public Service Commission (“Commission”)
makes the necessary findings to justify granting of such a certificate, and provided the conditions
contained within this stipulation are met.

Commission Decision
The baseline for establishing an appropriate rate of return on common equity are
established by the decisions of the United States Supreme Court in Bluefield and Hope,
which establish that the ROE should be set at a level (1) commensurate with returns on
investments in other firms having corresponding risks; (ii) sufficient to assure confidence
in DESC’s financial integrity; and (111) sufficient to maintain DESC’s creditworthiness and
ability to attract capital on reasonable terms.
The
Commission is the fact finder in rate proceedings and must balance the interests
of the using and consuming public with that of the utility appearing before it. Additionally,
the Commission’s determination of a fair rate of return must be based on reliable and
probative evidence in the record. As a result, this Commission is bound by the parameters
of evidence in the record, and it hereby carefully evaluates the evidence submitted in this
case as to what ROE the Company should be authorized the opportunity to earn.
In this case, after consideration of the record, the Commission concludes that it is
just, reasonable, and a fair balancing of the interests of the Company and its customers to
approve the ROE of 9.99% as set out in the Revenue Requirement Stipulation. An ROE of
9.99% is supported by the record before the Commission, as it is within the range of ROE
estimates recommended by Witness Baudino. The Commission gives significant weight to
the compromise of the Revenue Requirement Stipulating Parties in reaching the Revenue
Requirement Stipulation, and DESC witnesses’ testimony in support thereof. As such, an
ROE of 9.99% is a reasonable compromise in this proceeding.

A. STIPULATION OF TESTIMONY AND WAIVER OF CROSS-EXAMINATION
1.
The Parties and Intervenors who do not oppose, or take no position on, this Large
Load Stipulation agree to stipulate into the record before the Commission the pre-filed testimony
and exhibits (collectively, the “Stipulated Testimony”) of all witnesses identified in the Revenue
Requirement Stipulation without objection, change, or amendment with the exception of changes
comparable to those that would be presented via an errata sheet or through a witness noting a
correction consistent with this Large Load Stipulation. The Parties and Intervenors who do not
oppose, or take no position on, this Large Load Stipulation also agree to waive cross-examination
of all witnesses. Further, the Parties and Intervenors who do not oppose this Large Load
Stipulation reserve the right to engage in redirect examination of their respective witnesses as
necessary to respond to issues raised by the examination of their witnesses, if any, by the
Commission or opposing parties.
2.
The Parties and Intervenors who do not oppose, or take no position on, this Large
Load Stipulation agree that no additional evidence shall be offered in this proceeding other than
the Stipulated Testimony and Exhibits and this Large Load Stipulation itself, unless such
additional evidence (a) supports the Large Load Stipulation, (b) consists of changes comparable
to that which would be presented via an errata sheet or through a witness noting a correction or

The Parties expressly acknowledge that this settlement arises out of a heavily
contested matter, with significant disagreements remaining on various issues addressed in this
Large Load Stipulation. While the Parties have agreed to certain adjustments and methodologies
as part of the negotiated compromise and settlement among the Parties, no Party consents to any
characterization of this Large Load Stipulation as reflecting its views on the resolution of the
underlying issues. No Party waives any right to assert any position on these issues in any future
proceeding or docket before the Commission or in any court. This Large Load Stipulation is a
product of negotiation among the Parties, and no provision of this Large Load Stipulation shall be
strictly construed in favor of or against any Party. Specifically, the Parties shall not be bound by
the terms of this Large Load Stipulation in any respect in future proceedings.

court or Commission except insofar as such court or Commission is addressing litigation arising
out of the implementation of the terms herein or the approval of this Large Load Stipulation. This
Large Load Stipulation is not intended to establish and shall not be cited as precedent by any of
the Parties regarding any issue in any other proceeding or docket before this Commission or in any
court.

LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS
10.
DESC agrees to join and participate in the Large Load generic docket that will be
filed with the
Commission by June 1, 2026, as approved by the Commission in the Duke Energy
Progress, LLC and Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC respective Applications for Increases in Electric
Rates, Adjustment in Electric Rate Schedules and Tariffs, and Request for an Accounting Order
in Docket Nos. 2025-172-E and 2025-154-E.
11. | The purpose of the Large Load generic docket is to evaluate the issues associated
with new large load (50 MW or greater) additions including existing rate schedules, service
regulations, line extension policies, and interconnection rules. The Petition, filed by Duke Energy
Progress, LLC and Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, along with signatories to the Commission
approved Large Load Stipulation in Docket Nos. 2025-172-E and 2025-154-E, shall request that
the Commission allow interested parties to file or otherwise present comments on topics related to
new large load customers, including but not limited to:

title: SC PSC Order No. 2026-375 — Order Adopting Stipulation and Approving the Stage 2 Application - Act No. 41 of 2025 and S.C. Code Ann. Section 58-42-30 and the Establishment of Competitive Procurement Programs for Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC and Duke Energy Progress, LLC for En...
summary: Order Adopting Stipulation and Approving the Stage 2 Application - Act No. 41 of 2025 and S.C. Code Ann. Section 58-42-30 and the Establishment of Competitive Procurement Programs for Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC and Duke Energy Progress, LLC for Energy Storage Facilities to Be Located in South Carolina
text:
BEFORE
THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
OF SOUTH CAROLINA
DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
— ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
IN RE:
Act No. 41 of 2025 and S.C. Code
Ann.
Section
58-42-30
and
the
Establishment
of
Competitive
Procurement Programs for Duke
Energy Carolinas, LLC and Duke
Energy Progress, LLC for Energy
Storage Facilities to Be Located in
South Carolina
ORDER ADOPTING STIPULATION
AND APPROVING THE
STAGE 2 APPLICATION
INTRODUCTION
This matter
comes before the Public Service Commission of South Carolina
(Commission) on the Application ofDuke Energy Carolinas, LLC (DEC) and Duke Energy
Progress, LLC (DEP, and together with DEC, the Companies) for approval of the
Companies’ proposed 2026 Request for Proposals for South Carolina-Sited Standalone
Battery Storage (2026 SC Battery RFP or RFP) pursuant to Section
18 of the South
Carolina Energy Security Act (Act 41), including relevant provisions of S.C. Code Ann.
sections 58-42-10 and 58-42-30 (Stage 2 Application).
The Commission previously issued Order No. 2026-274 (Stage
1 Order), which
approved the Stage 1 Stipulation Agreement and resolved framework-level issues related
to the 2026 SC Battery RFP. Through the Stage
1 Order, the Commission approved the
general framework for the procurement of South Carolina-sited stand-alone energy storage 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
— ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 2
resources, including the use of separate utility-owned and third-party-owned procurement
tracks, the target procurement volumes, and the use of an Independent Evaluator.
This Stage 2 Order (Order) implements and supplements the Stage
1 Order. It
resolves the issues presented by the Companies’ Stage 2 Application, including the
proposed RFP documents, pro forma Energy Storage Service Agreement (ESSA), bid
evaluation framework, cost-effectiveness methodology, role of the Independent Evaluator,
and other related implementation issues for the 2026 SC Battery RFP. Except to the extent
expressly modified, clarified, or limited by this Stage 2 Order, the findings, conclusions,
and directives contained in the Stage
1 Order remain in full force and effect and are
incorporated herein by reference.
For the reasons set forth below, the Commission approves the Companies’ Stage 2
Application, subject to the findings, conclusions, modifications, conditions, and directives
contained in this Order. The Commission further approves the Stipulation Agreement
(Stipulation)
entered into by the Companies and Carolinas Clean Energy Business
Association (CCEBA), which addresses and resolves certain issues in the Companies’
Stage 2 Application. The Commission approves the Revised 2026 SC Battery RFP, as
modified by the Stipulation, for the competitive procurement of stand-alone energy storage
resources to be located in South Carolina, as consistent with S.C. Code Ann. sections 58-
42-10 and 58-42-30 as well as Order No. 2026-274.
Il.
APPLICABLE LAW
Act 41 established a statutory framework for the competitive procurement of stand-
alone energy storage resources to be located in South Carolina. §§ S.C. Code Ann. 58-42- 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
- ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 3
10, 58-42-30 (Supp. 2025). Sections 58-42-10 and 58-42-30 set forth specific standards for
the Commission’s review of the Companies’ Stage 2 Application.
Section 58-42-10 provides that it is in the public interest for electrical utilities to
competitively procure certain stand-alone storage additions to be located in South Carolina,
consistent with the utilities’
2023 Integrated Resource Plans (IRP) approved by the
Commission
or subsequent Commission-approved
annual
IRP updates,
with
such
resources intended to be in service by January 1, 2035. S.C. Code Ann. § 58-42-10(A).
Electrical utilities must procure stand-alone storage resources through at least a
biennial competitive procurement process consistent with the requirements of S.C. Code
Ann. section 58-42-30. S.C. Code Ann. § 58-42-10(B). The target procurement volume for
stand-alone energy storage may not exceed the portion of stand-alone storage in the most
recent Commission-approved IRP or annual IRP update that is equal to the portion of the
respective electrical utility’s peak load attributable to South Carolina customers. S.C. Code
Ann. § 58-42-30(A)(2).! The procurement of stand-alone energy storage facilities must
result in a reasonable balance of electrical utility ownership and independent third-party
ownership, as determined by the Commission. S.C. Code Ann. § 58-42-30(A)(4)(a).
Act 41 permits utility participation in the competitive procurement, subject to
certain protections. Specifically, “{a]n electrical utility and its affiliates may offer proposals
into the competitive procurement provided that appropriate safeguards are in place to
' Stand-alone energy storage facilities with a design capacity less than or equal to twenty megawatts and
intended primarily to address local reliability improvements or local capacity constraints are not subject to
the competitive procurement requirements of this section. S.C. Code Ann. § 58-42-30(A)(3). 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
— ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 4
ensure that such proposals do not receive any advantage in the bid evaluation process.”
S.C. Code Ann. § 58-42-30(A)(4)(b).
Act 41 also requires cost-effectiveness confirmation prior to final procurement
awards. The electrical utility must “confirm that the resources selected are cost-effective
using methodologies and current inputs reflected in the applicable integrated resource plan
or integrated resource plan update approved by the commission for that electrical utility[,]”
prior to making final awards. S.C. Code Ann. § 58-42-10(G). Section 58-42-30 also
provides that stand-alone storage facilities shall be subject to operational protocols,
equipment specifications, and inspections established by the electrical utility that are
necessary to ensure the reliability of the electrical utility system and requires information
regarding such resources to be provided to the Office of Regulatory Staff(ORS). S.C. Code
Ann. § 58-42-30(B).
Regarding cost recovery, Act 41 provides that electrical utility costs associated with
facilities owned by an independent third-party power producer shall be capitalized and
included within the electrical utility’s rate base for ratemaking purposes. S.C. Code Ann.
§ 58-42-30(A)(4)(b). Act 41 further provides that electrical utilities may recover costs
incurred through the competitive procurement of stand-alone energy storage through rates
established pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. § 58-27-870. S.C. Code Ann. § 58-42-30(C). S.C.
Code Ann. section 58-27-870 governs general rate proceedings before the Commission and
requires Commission approval of proposed rates.
In addition, S.C. Code Ann. section 58-37-40(C)(4) provides that the review and
acceptance of an IRP by the Commission, or the inclusion of any specific resource in an
accepted IRP, is not determinative of the reasonableness or prudence of the acquisition or 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E— ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 5
construction of any resource or the making of any expenditure. Ultimately, the electrical
utility retains the burden to show that its investments and expenditures are reasonable and
prudent when seeking cost recovery in rates.
Il.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY
On July 22, 2025, the Commission issued Order No. 2025-473, opening this Docket
pursuant to Act No. 41 and S.C. Code Ann. section 58-42-30 to address the establishment
of competitive procurement programs for Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC and Duke Energy
Progress, LLC for energy storage facilities to be located in South Carolina.
Preliminary Filings
On September 25, 2025, the Companies filed
a Letter Providing Procedural
Schedule and Requesting to Consolidate Dockets.
ORS filed
a letter notifying the
Commission that ORS did not object either to the Companies’ proposed procedural
schedule or to their request to consolidate dockets.
After being granted intervenor status
on September 29, 2025, CCEBA filed a letter notifying the Commission that it did not
object to the Companies’ proposed procedural schedule and request to consolidate dockets
but reserved the right to seek leave to file surreplies as appropriate.
On October 9, 2025,
the Commission
issued
Order No. 2025-636, approving the Companies’ proposed
procedural schedule, as amended, and request to consolidate dockets.
Notice and Petitions to Intervene
By letter dated December 5, 2025, the Clerk’s Office directed the Companies to
publish, on or before December 19, 2025, a Notice of Filing (Notice) in newspapers of
general circulation one time and provide Proof of Publication on or before January 9, 2026.
On January 2, 2026, the Companies filed the Publisher’s Affidavit, noting December 17, 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
— ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE6.
2025, as the publishing date for the Notice, and on January 7, 2026, the Companies filed
Affidavits of Publication for the Notice.
CCEBA filed
a timely Petition to Intervene.
The Petition to Intervene
was
unopposed and was granted by the Commission in Order No. 2025-111-H. No other
interested parties sought to intervene. ORS is a party of record in all proceedings before
the Commission pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. section 58-4-10(B) (Supp. 2025).
Stage 1 Application
On November 21, 2025, the Companies filed their Application for Approval of
Proposal for Competitive Procurement of South Carolina-Sited Energy Storage Resources
Under Act 41 (Stage
1 Application).
The Companies, ORS, and CCEBA participated in
Stage 1 of this proceeding, which addressed framework-level issues for the proposed 2026
SC Battery RFP. On January 15, 2026, ORS filed its Public Comments and CCEBA filed
its Comments
on the Companies’ Stage
1
Application.
On January 29, 2026,
the
Companies filed Reply Comments. On March 20, 2026, the Companies, ORS, and CCEBA
filed a Stipulation Agreement resolving certain Stage
1 issues. On April 8, 2026, the
Companies filed the Stipulation Testimony of witnesses Maura Farver and Heather Shirley
Smith. The
same day, CCEBA filed
a letter in lieu of testimony in support of the
Stipulation. On April 10, 2026, ORS filed
a letter stating the Stipulation “reflects
a
reasonable compromise of the Parties that creates a practical framework for the 2026
Battery RFP and
serves the public interest”. The Commission approved the Stage
1
Stipulation Agreement in Order No. 2026-274. In that Order, the Commission approved
the general framework for the 2026 SC Battery RFP and directed that additional proposals,
terms, methodologies, and details be addressed in Stage 2. 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
— ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 7
Stage 2 Application
On April 20, 2026, the Companies filed their Stage 2 Application, accompanied by
witness verification,” seeking Commission approval of the proposed 2026 SC Battery RFP,
including the proposed RFP documents, pro forma Energy Storage Services Agreement
(ESSA),
bid
evaluation
framework,
Independent
Evaluator role,
cost-effectiveness
methodology, and related RFP implementation details.
On May 18, 2026, ORS filed Verified Comments? addressing the
Companies’ Stage
2
Application
and
recommending
certain
conditions,
clarifications,
and
reporting
requirements. CCEBA also filed Comments
on May 18, 2026. The Companies filed
verified Reply Comments on June 1, 2026, including a Revised 2026 SC Battery RFP and
Pro Forma ESSA
On June 10, 2026, the Companies and CCEBA (the Stipulating Parties) entered into
a Stipulation, a copy of which is attached as Order Exhibit No. 1. The Stipulating Parties
agreed to terms applicable to ESSA projects and Utility-Ownership Track (UOT) projects,
among other items.
This Stage 2 Order supplements and implements Order No. 2026-274 and resolves
the Stage 2 issues necessary for the Companies to proceed with the 2026 SC Battery RFP
subject to the findings, conditions, and limitations set forth herein.
IV.
FINDINGS OF FACT
After review of the Stage 2 Application, the proposed 2026 SC Battery RFP
documents, the proposed pro forma ESSA, the comments filed by ORS and CCEBA, the
2 Witness Maura Farver filed a Verification of Stage 2 Application.
3 ORS Witness James Findlay Salter filed a Verification in support of ORS’s Comments on Stage 2. 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
— ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 8
Companies’ Reply Comments, the Stage 1 Stipulation Agreement, Order No. 2026-274,
the Stipulation, and the entire record in this proceeding, the Commission makes the
following findings of fact:
Preliminary Findings
1.
DEC and DEP are public utilities under the jurisdiction of the Commission.
2.
The Companies filed an Application on April 20, 2026, pursuant to S.C.
Code Ann. sections 58-42-10 and 58-42-30, seeking approval of their 2026 SC Battery
RFP.
3.
On May 15, 2026, the Commission issued Order No. 2026-274 approving
the Stage 1 Stipulation Agreement and resolving framework-level issues related to the 2026
SC Battery RFP.
4.
It is reasonable and appropriate for this Stage 2 Order to supplement and
implement Order No. 2026-274. Except to the extent expressly modified, clarified, or
limited by this Order, the findings, conclusions, and directives contained in Order No.
2026-274 remain in full force and effect and are incorporated herein by reference.
Approval of the 2026 SC Battery RFP
5.
The 2026 SC Battery RFP to competitively procure stand-alone energy
storage resources to be located in South Carolina, pursuant to $.C. Code Ann. section 58-
42-30 and Order No. 2026-274, is reasonable and appropriate for implementation, subject
to the modifications, conditions, and requirements set forth in this Order.
6.
The economic score for both ESSA track bids and UOT bids shall be
weighted 60 percent or greater. 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E —ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 9
7.
The Companies will assign non-economic scores, which will include a
combination of Development, Technology, and Operational Characteristics.
8.
For UOT bids,
the Companies
shall
include any applicable year-20
augmentation
costs
in the
levelized
cost of capacity analysis
where year-15
cell
replacement assumptions are used.
Cost-effectiveness Evaluation Framework
9,
The Companies’ proposed use of a levelized cost of capacity (LCOC)
comparison to the applicable IRP reference cost is a reasonable framework to evaluate cost-
effectiveness under S.C. Code Ann. section 58-42-10(G), subject to the modifications,
conditions, and requirements set forth in this Order.
10.
Before
making
final
awards,
the
Companies
shall
evaluate
cost-
effectiveness of the total portfolio of selected resources.
11.
If the weighted-average LCOC of the total portfolio materially exceeds the
applicable
IRP
reference cost, the Companies
shall provide
a written justification
explaining
why
the
selected
Finalists
remain
cost-effective
and
reasonable.
The
justification shall use the methodologies and current inputs reflected in the applicable
Commission-approved IRP or IRP update.
12.
If the portfolio
of
selected
resources
fails
this
cost
effectiveness
assessment, the Companies may determine ifthey no longer require the full 400 MW target
procurement volume to meet capacity reserve requirements. In this case, the Companies
may elect to reduce the total capacity volume ofselected resources until such change results
in a cost effective portfolio that supports resource adequacy. 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
—- ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 10
13.
The Companies
shall
consider
and
address
the results
of the
cost-
effectiveness evaluation when confirming final procurement volumes and final selected
resources for the 2026 SC Battery RFP. Because the ownership volumes agreed to in the
Stage 1 Stipulation are target volumes, and not strict ownership mandates, minimums, or
caps, adjustments to Finalists
or procurement track target volumes
are permitted if
supported by the cost-effectiveness evaluation and ifconsistent with the reasonable balance
requirements of S.C. Code Ann. section 58-42-30(A)(4)(a).
14.
Consistent with the
Companies’ stated intent to bring the results of the RFP
back to the Commission for evaluation and approval, and as a condition of this Order, the
Companies shall bring the results of the 2026 SC Battery RFP back to the Commission for
review before making final awards. The filing shall include, at
a minimum, the selected
Finalists,
final
procurement
volumes,
cost-effectiveness
evaluation,
Independent
Evaluator’s
post-solicitation
report,
and
sufficient
supporting
documentation
to
demonstrate compliance with the requirements, conditions, limitations, and directives set
forth in this Order.
Role of the Independent Evaluator
15.
The role of the Independent Evaluator during the 2026 SC Battery RFP pre-
solicitation activities and throughout the RFP process,
as described in the Stage 2
Application and RFP documents, is reasonable and appropriate, subject to the requirements
set forth in this Order.
16.
The Independent Evaluator’s post-solicitation report shall include the
results of the cost-effectiveness evaluation required by S.C. Code Ann. section 58-42-
10(G), including a description ofthe analysis, any modeling performed, and an explanation 

DOCKET NO. 2025-217-E
— ORDER NO. 2026-375
JULY 2, 2026
PAGE 11
of any IRP inputs considered that differ from the base case Near Term Action Plan
assumptions in the applicable Commission-approved IRP or IRP update.
17.
The Independent Evaluator’s post-solicitation report shall also address
whether the RFP process and bid evaluation maintained appropriate safeguards to ensure
that UOT track proposals did not receive any advantage in the bid evaluation process.
Cost-Recovery Methodology for RFP Modeling Assumptions
18.
S.C. Code Ann. section 58-42-30(A)(4)(b) requires electrical utility costs
associated with facilities owned by an independent third-party power producer to be
capitalized and included within the electrical utility’s rate base for ratemaking purposes.
19.
For purposes of evaluating ESSA track bids in the 2026 SC Battery RFP, it
is reasonable and appropriate for the Companies to include a transparent RFP modeling
assumption reflecting the Companies’ proposed pro forma adjustment in regulatory
reporting and cost-recovery proceedings during the ESSA
contract
term.
The RFP
modeling assumption is authorized solely for bid evaluation and cost-effectiveness review

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF SOUTH CAROLINA

DOCKET NO. 2026-138-E ORDER NO. 2026-141-H (A) 

JULY 6, 2026

for the Purpose of Receiving Comments Addressing Large Load Additions) 

MATTER UNDER CONSIDERATION: This Amended Standing Hearing Officer Directive 
(SHOD) amends the SHOD to correct two typographical errors and substitution of “DCA” for 
“Sierra Club” in last two sentences from the first paragraph under Hearing Officer’s Action.” 
There is no other change to the SHOD concerning the Petition to Intervene of the South Carolina 
Department of Consumer Affairs (DCA) filed on June 17, 2026. (DCA Petition to Intervene) 

HEARING OFFICER’S ACTION: This matter comes before the Hearing Officer on the timely 
filed Petition to Intervene of the South Carolina Department of Consumer Affairs (DCA) in this 
docket. On June 12, 2026, the Clerk’s Office of the Commission set the deadline to file a Petition 
to Intervene in this docket as Monday, July 20, 2026. DCA seeks to intervene in this proceeding 
with full rights to participate as a party of record. There was no objection filed in this docket 
opposing the Petition of DCA to Intervene as provided by S.C. Regs. 103-825A(3). The Hearing 
Officer finds that the Petition to Intervene by DCA is timely filed. 

Having determined that the Petition to Intervene was timely filed, it must next be determined that 
the petitioning party has clear factual support or grounds for the proposed intervention. S.C. Code 
Ann. Regs. 103-825A(3) requires that parties filing a Petition to Intervene in a matter pending 
before the South Carolina Public Service Commission must set forth clearly and concisely: 
(a) The facts from which the nature of the petitioner's alleged right or interest can be 
determined; 
(b) The grounds of the proposed intervention; and 
(c) The position of the petitioner in the proceeding. 

The next question to determine is whether the petitioning party or parties state clear factual support 
or grounds for the proposed intervention. 

The Commission opened this generic docket on May 27, 2026, when Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC 
(DEC) and Duke Energy Progress, LLC (DEP) filed a Petition with the Commission. DEC and 
DEP stated that the Petition arises from the Stipulations approved in Commission Orders No. 2025-
757 and 2025-769. These Orders stated in the Stipulations that DEC and DEP agreed to request 
‘that the Commission open a generic docket for the purpose of evaluating issues associated with 
new large load (50 MW or greater) additions’ and ‘request[ing] that the Commission accept 
comments from interested parties’ in this generic docket.” DEC/DEP Transmittal Letter, dated 

AMENDED STANDING HEARING OFFICER DIRECTIVE ORDER NO. 2026-141-H (A) 
DOCKET NO. 2026-138-E 
JULY 6, 2026 
PAGE 2 OF 2 

May 27, 2026, p. 1. On June 12, 2026, the Commission directed the Chief Clerk to discuss a 
procedural schedule with all interested parties so that one can be proposed on June 25, 2026 for 
consideration by the Commission. Order No. 2026-334. Meanwhile, using her ministerial 
authority, the Commission Chief Clerk sent a transmittal letter and Notice of Filing directing DEC 
and DEP publish the Notice of Filing, which included the aforementioned deadline to file a Petition 
to Intervene. 

Pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. § 37-6-604(C), DCA “may intervene as a party to advocate for the 
interest of consumers before the Public Service Commission . . . in such matters as the Consumer 
Advocate deems necessary and appropriate.” S.C. Code Ann. § 37-6-604(C) (2018); see also, 
DCA Petition to Intervene, p. 1, ¶ 2. Additionally, subsection (A)(1) of Section 37-6-604 provides 
that the Consumer Advocate may “provide legal representation of the consumer interest before 
state and federal regulatory agencies which undertake to fix rates or prices for consumer products 
or services.” S.C. Code Ann. § 37-6-604(A)(1) (2018). In this capacity, DCA petitions to 
intervene as a formal party of record in Docket No. 2026-138-E to advocate for the interest of 
consumers. Additionally, DCA “works to avoid excessive, inadequate, and unwarranted rate 
increases; however, a position has not yet been fully developed on this matter.” Id., ¶ 3. DCA 
reserves the right to set forth a position more fully as this proceeding moves forward. Id. 

From the discussion above and assertions in the Petition of the South Carolina Department of 
Consumer Affairs to Intervene, this Hearing Officer holds that the South Carolina Department of 
Consumer Affairs has satisfied the criteria for intervention pursuant to Regulation 103-825A(3) 
and that clear factual support and/or grounds for the intervention are clearly provided and 
established. No party(s) of record objected to this Petition to Intervene. There is no prejudice 
against the other parties of record. The Petitioner’s interest in these matters can clearly be 
discerned from the Petition. Accordingly, the Petition to Intervene of the South Carolina 
Department of Consumer Affairs is hereby granted in this Docket. The South Carolina Department 
of Consumer Affairs is now a formal party of record and it shall actively participate in this 
proceeding with all rights as a party of record. 

This ends the Hearing Officer’s Directive.

MATTER UNDER CONSIDERATION: Petition to Intervene of Google, LLC (Google) filed 
on June 22, 2026. (Petition to Intervene) 
HEARING OFFICER’S ACTION: This matter comes before the Hearing Officer on the timely 
filed Petition to Intervene of Google, LLC (Google) in this docket. On June 12, 2026, the Clerk’s 
Office of the Commission set the deadline to file a Petition to Intervene in this docket as Monday, 
July 20, 2026. Google seeks to intervene in this proceeding with full rights to participate as a party 
of record. There was no objection filed in this docket opposing the Petition of Google to Intervene 
as provided by S.C. Regs. 103-825A(3). The time for the Applicants or any other party of record 
in this Docket to file an objection or response to the Joint Petition to Intervene has expired. There 
was no Response or objection filed. The Hearing Officer finds that the Petition to Intervene by 
Google is timely filed. 
Having determined that the Petition to Intervene was timely filed, it must next be determined that 
the petitioning party has clear factual support or grounds for the proposed intervention. S.C. Code 
Ann. Regs. 103-825A(3) requires that parties filing a Petition to Intervene in a matter pending 
before the South Carolina Public Service Commission must set forth clearly and concisely: 
(a) The facts from which the nature of the petitioner's alleged right or interest can be
determined;
(b) The grounds of the proposed intervention; and
(c) The position of the petitioner in the proceeding.
The next question to determine is whether the petitioning party or parties state clear factual support 
or grounds for the proposed intervention. 
The Commission opened this generic docket on May 27, 2026, when Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC 
(DEC) and Duke Energy Progress, LLC (DEP) filed a Petition with the Commission. DEC and 
DEP stated that the Petition arises from the Stipulations approved in Commission Orders No. 2025-
757 and 2025-769. The Stipulations adopted by these Orders state that DEC and DEP agreed to 
request ‘that the Commission open a generic docket for the purpose of evaluating issues associated 
with new large load (50 MW or greater) additions’ and ‘request[ing] that the Commission accept 
comments from interested parties’ in this generic docket.” DEC/DEP Transmittal Letter, dated 
May 27, 2026, p. 1. On June 12, 2026, the Commission directed the Chief Clerk to discuss a

DOCKET NO. 2026-138-E 
JULY 6, 2026 
PAGE 2 OF 2 
procedural schedule with all interested parties so that one can be proposed on June 25, 2026 for 
consideration by the Commission. Order No. 2026-334. Meanwhile, using her administrative 
authority, the Commission Chief Clerk sent a transmittal letter and Notice of Filing directing DEC 
and DEP publish the Notice of Filing, which included the aforementioned deadline to file a Petition 
to Intervene. 

In support of its Petition, Google asserts the following: 

■ 
Google is a “provider of online services and products. In connection with these business 
operations, Google, through its affiliates, is developing one or more data centers and related 
infrastructure in the service territory of Dominion Energy South Carolina (“DESC”).” 
Petition to Intervene, p. 1, ¶ 2. 
■ 
Data Centers are high-load factor facilities that use energy every day, all day. Id., p. 1, ¶ 3. 
■ 
It is critically important to Google’s data center operations to have the availability of an 
adequate and reliable electric power supply at reasonable rates, terms, and conditions. Id., 
p. 1, ¶ 4. 
■ 
Any change or modification to DESC's electric rates and terms of service may have 
material financial impacts on Google’s operations in DESC territory. Id., p. 1, ¶ 5. 
■ 
Google was a signatory, with DESC and other parties of record, to the Large Load 
Stipulation filed in the rate case of DESC (i.e., Docket No. 2025-325-E) and adopted by 
the Commission in Order No. 2026-374. Id., p. 2, ¶ 5. 
■ 
Google has participated in numerous large load dockets throughout the United States and 
is interested in any potential changes to the terms, conditions, and rates for a high energy 
user of DESC like Google. Any changes may have a material financial impact on the 
operations of Google. Id., p. 2, ¶ 7. 
■ 
As a high use customer of DESC with significant economic investment in DESC’s service 
territory, Google has a direct, substantial, and vital interest in the outcome of this 
proceeding. Id., p. 2, ¶ 8. 
■ 
No other party can adequately represent Google’s interest in this matter. Id. 

From the discussion above and assertions in the Petition of Google, LLC, to Intervene, this Hearing 
Officer holds that Google, LLC, has satisfied the criteria for intervention pursuant to Regulation 
103-825A(3) and that clear factual support and/or grounds for the intervention are clearly provided 
and established. No party(s) of record objected to this Petition to Intervene. There is no prejudice 
against the other parties of record. The Petitioner’s interest in these matters can clearly be 
discerned from the Petition. Accordingly, the Petition to Intervene of Google, LLC, is hereby 
granted in this Docket. Google, LLC, is now a formal party of record and it shall actively 
participate in this proceeding with all rights as a party of record. 

This ends the Hearing Officer’s Directive.

title: SC PSC Order No. 2026-155H — Standing Hearing Officer Directive Order Granting Confidential Treatment - Application of CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc. for Designation as an Eligible Telecommunications Carrier in the State of South Carolina
summary: Standing Hearing Officer Directive Order Granting Confidential Treatment - Application of CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc. for Designation as an Eligible Telecommunications Carrier in the State of South Carolina
text:
PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF SOUTH CAROLINA 

STANDING HEARING OFFICER DIRECTIVE 

DOCKET NO. 2021-15-C ORDER NO. 2026-155-H 

JULY 7, 2026 

STANDING HEARING OFFICER: C. Jo Anne Wessinger Hill, Esquire 

DOCKET DESCRIPTION: DOCKET NO. 2021-15-C – Application of CarolinaConnect 
Cooperative, Inc. for Designation as an Eligible Telecommunications Carrier in the State of South 
Carolina 

MATTER UNDER CONSIDERATION: Request by CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc. 
(CarolinaConnect) for the Commission to grant Confidential Treatment of its Annual Eligible 
Telecommunications Carrier Report required to be filed with the Commission, along with the 
attached copy of its filed FCC Form 481 designated as Exhibit A in the annual Report. This 
Request was filed on June 24, 2026 (Request). 

HEARING OFFICER’S ACTION: This matter comes before the Hearing Officer on the 
Request of CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc. (CarolinaConnect), seeking Confidential Treatment 
for its annual Eligible Telecommunications Carrier Report (ETC Report) required to be filed with 
the Commission, along with the attached copy of its filed FCC Form 481 which was included as 
Exhibit A to the ETC Report. This Request, along a copy of the information filed under seal, was 
filed on June 24, 2026, with a redacted public version. 

The Request is made pursuant to the South Carolina Freedom of Information Act, S.C. Code Ann. 
§§ 30-4-10, et. seq., and S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-804(S)(2). The Request is also in compliance 
with Commission Orders No. 2005-226, 2020-490, 2023-859, and 2025-321. In its request for 
confidential treatment, CarolinaConnect identified and designated the confidential information 
which it maintains to be proprietary, highly sensitive, and confidential. Request, p. 1. 

In submitting the Request, CarolinaConnect asserts the need to protect the redacted information 
from public disclosure because the confidential information is proprietary and of a commercially 
sensitive nature. The identified and designated information is confidential information that is not 
known, or available, to the public or the company’s competitors. If the information is publicly 
disclosed, CarolinaConnect will be competitively harmed from such disclosure and risk other 
carriers obtaining information not publicly known or available. In fact, public disclosure of such 
highly confidential information would allow competitors to obtain economic value from such 
disclosure. CarolinaConnect also asks for the Commission to exclude this information from public 
disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, S.C. Code Ann. §§ 30-4-10, et. seq. 

Commission Regulation 103-804(S)(2) provides that the Commission, within its discretion, can 
determine what matters are placed and available in the public record on the Commission’s Docket 
Management System (DMS). S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-804(S)(2) (2012). Likewise, the 
Commission has discretion to determine what matters are exempt from public disclosure, including 
exemption from release under the Freedom of Information Act, S.C. Code Ann. §§ 30-4-10 et. seq. 

STANDING HEARING OFFICER DIRECTIVE NO. 2026-155-H 
JULY 7, 2026 
PAGE 2 OF 2 

Disclosure of confidential and proprietary information can cause competitive harm to a company 
when such information is not available to the public. Considering the Request of CarolinaConnect 
Cooperative, Inc., and its actions in compliance with Commission Orders No. 2005-226, 2020-
490, 2023-859, and applicable laws, the Hearing Officer finds and concludes that confidential 
treatment is warranted: 

(1) for the proprietary and commercially sensitive information identified and marked by 
CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc., as confidential in the filing of its annual Eligible 
Telecommunications Carrier Report and the attached copy of its filed FCC Form 481 
which is included as Exhibit A in the annual ETC Report. 

Accordingly, the Request for Confidential Treatment is granted as requested by 
CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc., for the information and data designated as confidential 
in its annual ETC Report and the attached copy of its filed FCC Form 481 included as 
Exhibit A to the annual ETC Report. 

The Hearing Officer further finds and concludes that the non-redacted confidential version of its 
annual ETC Report and the FCC Form 481 filed by CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc., are exempt 
from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, S.C. Code Ann. §§ 30-4-10 et. seq. 
Therefore, the Request is granted to exempt the information designated as confidential in the 
annual ETC Report and in the FCC Form 481 filed by CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc., from 
disclosure pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act. 

The Commission shall maintain as confidential and/or exempt from disclosure under the Freedom 
of Information Act the non-redacted confidential designated version of certain information 
identified and marked as confidential and proprietary by CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc., in its 
annual ETC Report and in the FCC Form 481 unless or until the Commission rules designated and 
identified information is not entitled to protection from public disclosure, or CarolinaConnect 
Cooperative, Inc., agrees that such information is no longer confidential, commercially sensitive, 
or proprietary. 

On behalf of the Commission, this Hearing Officer further accepts for filing both the nonredacted 
confidential version filed under seal and the redacted public version of the annual Eligible 
Telecommunications Carrier Report and the attached copy of the filed FCC Form 481 included 
with the Report as Exhibit A as filed with the Commission by CarolinaConnect Cooperative, Inc., 
in this Docket. 

This concludes the Hearing Officer’s Directive. 

---XXX---

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF SOUTH CAROLINA 

AMENDED STANDING HEARING OFFICER DIRECTIVE 

DOCKET NO. 2026-163-E ORDER NO. 2026-154-H(A) 

JULY 8, 2026 

STANDING HEARING OFFICER: C. Jo Anne Wessinger Hill, Esquire 

DOCKET DESCRIPTION: DOCKET NO. 2026-163-E – Power Purchase Agreement Between 
Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC and Chester PV1, LLC 

MATTER UNDER CONSIDERATION: Request by Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (DEC) for 
the Commission to grant Confidential Treatment to the Power Purchase Agreement (“PPA” or 
“Agreement”) between Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC (DEC) and Chester PV1, LLC (Chester PV1) 
filed on June 25, 2026 (DEC Letter/Request). 

HEARING OFFICER’S ACTION: The amendment to the July 7, 2026 Standing Officer 
Directive when compared with this July 8, 2026 Amended Standing Hearing Officer Directive is 
a correction of an inadvertent typographical error replacing the name of the Duke Company from 
“Progress” in certain places with the name of “Carolinas” to reflect Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, 
as described in the docket above. There is no change related to the Request for Confidential 
Treatment as granted. 

This matter comes before the Hearing Officer on a Request by DEC pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. 
section 58-41-20(E)(1), S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-804 and Commission Order No. 2005-226, as 
amended by Orders No. 2020-490 and 2023-859, seeking Confidential Treatment of certain 
portions of the Power Purchase Agreement between DEC and Chester PV1. Section 58-41-
20(E)(1) mandates that all electric “utilities shall file with the commission power purchase 
agreements entered into pursuant to PURPA, resulting from voluntary negotiation of contracts 
between an electrical utility and a small power producer not eligible for the standard offer.” S.C. 
Code Ann. § 58-41-20(E)(1) (Supp. 2025) (emphasis added). 

In submitting the filing, DEC asserts that “[d]ue to the commercial sensitivity and proprietary 
nature of certain portions of the Agreement, DEC respectfully requests that the Commission find 
that, pursuant to S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 103-804(S)(2) and S.C. Code Ann. § 30-4-40(a)(1), certain 
provisions of the Agreement are exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, 
S.C. Code Ann. §§ 30-4-10 et seq.” DEC Letter/Request, p. 1. DEC further asserts that 
confidentiality is sought for the identified confidential information and relevant provisions of the 
Agreement for which DEC “derives economic value” from such information “not being generally 
known to, and not being readily ascertainable by proper means, by other persons who would be 
able to obtain economic value from its disclosure.” Id. Additionally, DEC states that the redacted 
and confidential provisions are “confidential pricing and conditions, as well as delivery parameters 
and details of the operating characteristics of the facility, all of which are proprietary and specific 
to this counter-party [Chester PV1].” Id. DEC further states that the specific redactions and 
confidentiality in the Agreement were mutually reviewed and agreed upon by both DEC and 
Chester PV1, as well as the parties agreeing not to disclose any term of these confidential 
provisions to a third party without the prior written consent of the other party. Id.

DOCKET NOS. 2026-163-E 
JULY 8, 2026

Commission Regulation 103-804(S)(2) provides that the Commission, within its discretion, can 
determine what matters are placed and available in the public record on the DMS. S.C. Code Ann. 
Regs. 103-804(S)(2) (2012). Likewise, the Commission has discretion to determine what matters 
are exempt from public disclosure, including exemption from release under the Freedom of 
Information Act, S.C. Code Ann. §§ 30-4-10 et seq. Id. 

In support of the Request and in protection of this information, DEC complied with the 
requirements of Commission Order 2005-226, as amended by Orders No. 2020-490 and 2023-859. 
Additionally, DEC provided a confidential version and a redacted public version of the Agreement 
to the Commission and the Office of Regulatory Staff. There were no objections to the Request 
for Confidential Treatment requested by DEC. 

Considering the Request of DEC and acts in compliance with Orders No. 2005-226, 2020-490, 
and 2023-859, the Hearing Officer finds that confidential treatment of the Power Purchase 
Agreement between Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, and Chester PV1, LLC, is warranted. 
Accordingly, the Request for Confidential Treatment filed by Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, 
is granted as requested. The Power Purchase Agreement between Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, 
and Chester PV1, LLC, is exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, S.C. 
Code Ann. §§ 30-4-10 et seq. The Commission shall maintain the confidential version of this 
Agreement as confidential unless or until the Commission rules such information is not entitled to 
protection from public disclosure, or Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, and Chester PV1, LLC, agree 
that such information is no longer confidential, commercially sensitive, or proprietary. 

The Hearing Officer further accepts for filing the Power Purchase Agreement between Duke 
Energy Carolinas, LLC, and Chester PV1, LLC, on behalf of the Commission. 

This concludes the Hearing Officer’s Directive.
